items.title: Gene Bertoncini interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: probably would have delayed my most important work which is getting into the solo work and the duo work with Mike.

ctx.x: I’ll be darned. You finally said no once and it was a —

Well you know I’m not too sure — it wasn’t a mistake because I think I could not have resisted the success that that group had. I would have gone out on the road probably and done concerts with them and probably would have delayed my most important work which is getting into the solo work and the duo work with Mike.
Yeah. That’s a good story though. Do you still do a lot of studio work, or you’ve cut back on that?

items.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: And I think that’s one of the things that really encouraged me to keep working with Gene is we had material worked out.

ctx.x: What is it about his playing that’s kept you two together for so many years?

Well I think number one he gets jobs, but I think the thing is that he has a great sense of arranging for the two instruments, again, featuring the bass in a very nice way. And he encouraged me to do things with the bow that I hadn’t done, and he came up with — really, most of the time I don’t like jazz and classical mixed together. I find that usually it doesn’t work for one reason or the other. It takes away from both. But his arrangements seem to work as far as the integrity of both. The classical part was…

I really enjoy hearing a combo or small ensemble that is basically a jazz unit but every once in a while they’ll do something that you know has been arranged and rehearsed. I think it really adds a lot of the performance that that group took the time to do that.
